extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of media/cultural studies, communication researchers, and those studying television/news production and reception
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical framework for analyzing broadcast (especially televisual) communication as an articulated circuit of production, circulation, distribution/consumption and reproduction, emphasizing the distinct moments of encoding and decoding and the ideological work of codes. Useful for critically assessing how messages are produced, signified, received and transformed into social practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circuit as articulated moments (production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of communication as a 'complex structure in dominance' produced through linked but distinctive moments – production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a communicative instance, identify and treat each moment (production, circulation, distribution/consumption, reproduction) as a distinct modality with its own conditions; examine how articulation between these moments sustains or interrupts the circuit (e.g., breaks in passage of forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discursive 'message form' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'raw' historical event cannot be transmitted in itself; an event must be signified within discursive (aural-visual/televisual) forms — 'the event must become a "story" before it can become a communicative event.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how events are transformed into message-forms via the formal rules of language/discourse and how that transformation affects what can be communicated; consider what is lost, emphasized, or re-framed in the transposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encoding and decoding as determinate, relatively autonomous moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Encoding (production side) and decoding (reception side) are determinate moments in the communicative process; each has relative autonomy and its own modality and conditions of existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze encoding practices separately from decoding practices; do not assume a one-to-one mapping between them. Examine institutional and technical constraints on encoding and the cultural/ideological resources audiences use to decode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material/institutional conditions of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Production requires material instruments ('means'), technical infrastructure and specific social/production relations (organization, professional ideologies, routines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the institutional structures, professional practices, selection of personnel, technical infrastructures and access patterns that shape the encoded message (e.g., how production draws topics and agendas from wider socio-cultural formations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-entry of reception into production via feedbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulation and reception are 'moments' of production and are reincorporated into production via skewed and structured feedbacks; consumption/reception is itself moment of the production process in a larger sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace feedback loops (audience responses, ratings, institutional reactions) and how reception outcomes influence subsequent encoding/production decisions; consider asymmetries in these feedbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: No necessary equivalence between meaning structures (symmetry/asymmetry of codes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning structures at encoding (meaning structures 1) and decoding (meaning structures 2) may not be identical; degrees of 'symmetry/asymmetry' (equivalence) depend on relations and positions of encoder and decoder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the degree of fit between encoding and decoding codes; identify systematic distortions arising from lack of equivalence rather than treating them as random misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject simple behaviourist models of media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Television programmes are not simple behavioural inputs; semiotic/paradigmatic approaches are required to understand content and reception rather than low-level behaviourist explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating messages as direct causal stimuli; instead analyze the semiotic operations and interpretive frameworks that mediate any effects or 'uses' of media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Televisual sign as composite (visual + aural) and iconic but coded
rubrics_metrics.description: The televisual sign combines visual and aural discourses and is 'iconic' (posseses some properties of the thing represented) but remains a coded sign — there is no 'degree zero' in language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat visual and aural elements as coded practices; interrogate how iconicity is produced through codes and how it may create illusions of 'natural' representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalized codes and habituation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain codes may be so widely distributed and learned early that they appear 'natural' (naturalized), but this effect conceals the coding practices and ideological operations involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify presumed 'natural' perceptions and unpack the underlying codes and habituations; question taken-for-granted meanings that function as naturalized perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denotation and connotation as analytic distinction (both usually present)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denotation (literal aspects that appear near-universal) and connotation (associative, changeable meanings) are analytic tools; most signs combine denotative and connotative aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish denotative and connotative elements in analysis for analytic clarity, but avoid reifying them as separate realities; examine how connotative extensions open signs to ideological articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connotation as site of ideological interventions
rubrics_metrics.description: At the connotative level signs intersect with deep cultural semantic codes and acquire active ideological dimensions; connotation is where meanings are most transformable and contested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on connotative fields to see how ideologies are inscribed, accentuated or contested; use examples (advertising sweater connotations) to show how associative meanings are mobilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polysemy versus pluralism and hierarchy of connotative codes
rubrics_metrics.description: Signs are polysemic (open to multiple connotations) but connotative codes are not equal; cultures impose classified, hierarchically organized domains with 'preferred readings' embedded with social order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map the range of possible connotative readings but identify dominant/preferred meanings and the institutional/political ordering that privileges them; do not confuse multiplicity of meanings (polysemy) with democratic pluralism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of discourses 'in dominance' and preferred readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Discourses are 'structured in dominance' — certain semantic domains and mappings are institutionally privileged, carrying legitimacy and 'taken-for-granted' status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how dominant cultural orders produce preferred readings; trace the institutional, political and ideological imprints that make some readings normative and others marginal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative work and performative rules (competence, logics-in-use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicative practice involves performative interpretative work — rules of competence and use that actively enforce or prefer one semantic domain over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine the routines, conventions and interpretative competencies that producers and audiences draw upon to enforce particular readings; consider how professional practices delimit possible decodings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematically distorted communication (not merely 'selective perception')
rubrics_metrics.description: When audiences fail to take meaning as intended, this is often due to operating in different codes producing systematic distortions — 'selective perception' explanations are inadequate because patterns cluster across individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for patterned, clustered divergences between intended and actual readings that reflect structural/code differences rather than random individual variation; critique 'selective perception' as an insufficient explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three hypothetical decoding positions: dominant-hegemonic, negotiated, oppositional
rubrics_metrics.description: Decodings may typically fall into three positions: (1) dominant-hegemonic — viewer decodes the connoted meaning as encoded; (2) negotiated — accepts hegemonic definitions generally but adapts in local/situational ways; (3) oppositional — comprehends encoded meaning but decodes it within an alternative framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In empirical work, test for these positions in audience readings; use them to explain misunderstandings and political moments when negotiated readings shift into oppositional readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional code distinct from but operating within hegemony
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'professional code' (metacode) governs technical, presentational and professional transformations of content; it is relatively independent but operates within the hegemony and often reproduces dominant meanings by framing them as neutral or technical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate how professional norms (visual quality, presentational values, selection of formats/personnel) configure messages and how such norms may obscure ideological reproduction by appearing neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decode political/ideological struggle in moments of oppositional readings
rubrics_metrics.description: Oppositional decodings are politically significant and correspond to moments when normally negotiated signification is contested and re-signified within alternative frameworks ('politics of signification').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when and how audiences retotalize messages in oppositional ways; treat these moments as sites of ideological struggle with implications for broadcasting institutions and elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: No degree-zero or purely natural representation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no degree zero in language' — 'naturalism' or 'realism' is the product of specific articulations of language on the real, not transparent representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question claims of pure or transparent representation in visual media; analyze the conventions and codes producing apparent realism.
